text:
Marshall Rifai got his first NHL goal late in the third period, a slap shot at 16:58 that put Toronto up 6-2 and capped a rout. It was also the least likely goal of the night, a 2% chance by the model's count. The result flattered the Maple Leafs, though, and the gap was easy to see.

Columbus deserved to win this one. That means that in 68% of simulated replays of every shot, the Blue Jackets came out ahead. They took 65 shot attempts to Toronto's 43 and put 37 shots on goal to the Leafs' 22. In expected goals, which measure the quality of chances, Columbus led 3.61 to 2.49. The Leafs won the first period by that measure, then the Blue Jackets took over, and in the third they out-chanced Toronto 1.53 to 0.35. Damon Severson had a 28% look in the first period that Anthony Stolarz stopped, and Stolarz made 35 saves on 37 shots. By goals saved above expected, he stole 1.61 goals.

The other end told the opposite story. Toronto scored four times in the second period, and Jet Greaves, who relieved Cam Talbot, gave up 2.9 goals more than his 19 shots deserved. Easton Cowan (a short-handed goal and two assists) and Jack Roslovic (a goal and two assists) were two of the stars, with Auston Matthews the other. The Leafs scored once on five power plays and Columbus went 0 for 6. The facts don't include either team's streak or record, so this one stands as a single night's result: Toronto took the points on efficiency, and Columbus lost despite controlling the game.
